content: System change interventions for smoking cessation are organizational policies and practices aimed at systematically identifying smokers and offering them evidence-based treatments for nicotine dependence as part of routine care. These interventions are designed to enhance the delivery of smoking cessation support in healthcare settings and improve cessation outcomes for individuals who utilize these services. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of system change interventions implemented in healthcare settings in increasing smoking cessation rates, improving the provision of smoking cessation care, or both. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed in February 2016 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO. Additionally, clinical trial registries, such as the WHO clinical trial registry and the US National Institute of Health (NIH) clinical trial registry, were searched. Grey literature and bibliographies of relevant publications were also examined. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cluster-RCTs, quasi-RCTs, and interrupted time series studies that assessed system change interventions. These interventions had to involve the identification of all smokers and the subsequent offering of evidence-based nicotine dependence treatments. Data were extracted from eligible studies using a standardized form, focusing on study settings, participants, interventions, and outcomes of interest. Smoking cessation outcomes were defined using the strictest available criteria for abstinence. System-level outcomes included the assessment and documentation of smoking status, the provision of advice to quit or cessation counseling, referrals to quitline services, enrollment in quitline programs, and the prescribing of cessation medications. The risk of bias in each study was assessed using the Cochrane Handbook, and studies were categorized as having a high, low, or unclear risk of bias. Due to significant heterogeneity among the studies, a narrative synthesis was used to describe the effectiveness of the interventions on various outcomes. Seven cluster-randomized controlled studies were included in the review. The quality of evidence was rated as very low or low, depending on the outcome, based on the GRADE standard. The evidence for the effectiveness of these interventions in achieving smoking abstinence at the longest follow-up was inconclusive, as was the evidence for the prescribing of smoking cessation medications. Four studies assessed changes in the provision of smoking cessation counseling, with three studies favoring the intervention. Significant improvements were observed in the documentation of smoking status (one study), referrals to quitline services (two studies), and enrollment in quitline programs (two studies). Other secondary outcomes, such as asking about tobacco use (three studies) and advising patients to quit smoking (three studies), also showed some positive effects. The authors concluded that while system change interventions for smoking cessation may not significantly increase cessation rates, they do appear to improve process outcomes, such as the documentation of smoking status, the provision of cessation counseling, and referrals to smoking cessation services. However, the limited amount of available research prevents strong conclusions from being drawn. Further high-quality research is needed to better understand the impact of system change interventions on both smoking cessation rates and system-level outcomes.
